messages.content: I cried when my mom had to go and now I can't stop. When will she be back?

Crying when someone you love leaves is completely normal, and it shows how much you care about your mom. She didn't go far — she might be in the waiting room, getting a coffee, or taking a quick rest, because taking care of you takes a lot of energy for grown-ups too. Your nurse knows how to reach her if you need her right away. You can also press the call button on your bed and ask. She'll be back as soon as she can, and until then, every single person in this building is here to help keep you safe.
I don't want any more needles. I already had two and that's enough.

Two needles is a lot, and it makes total sense that you don't want any more. Your care team knows exactly how you're feeling — you're allowed to tell them that too. Here at Children's Hospital there's something called the Comfort Promise, which means your team will do everything they can to make things hurt less. That includes numbing cream on your skin before anything goes in, so you barely feel the poke. You can also ask your nurse how many more needle things are planned, so you're not surprised. You're being so brave, and your feelings about it matter.
Everything smells different here and it makes me feel yucky.

You're right, hospitals do smell different from home — it's mostly the cleaning products they use to keep everything really safe and germ-free for all the kids here. That smell can feel a bit overwhelming, especially if you're already not feeling great. If it bothers you a lot, you can ask a nurse to open a window if possible, or bring something from home that smells nice — like a favourite lotion, a stuffed animal, or even a piece of clothing that smells like home. Some kids find that helps a lot.
What if I get scared in the night and nobody comes?

Someone will always come — that's a promise. There are nurses here all night long, every single night. They don't go home like other people do. Right next to your bed there's a call button, and the moment you press it, a nurse gets notified and comes to check on you. You don't have to be in a big emergency to press it — if you're scared, that's a completely good reason. Some kids keep the call button in their hand when they're trying to sleep, just so they know it's right there. You will never be left alone.
I heard the doctor talking outside my room and they said something about my blood. Is something really bad happening to me?

It can be really scary to hear grown-ups talking about you when you don't have all the words to understand what they mean. But here's the thing — doctors talk about blood tests all the time, because blood is like a little message from your body that tells them how you're doing. It doesn't mean something really bad is happening. It usually means they're checking. The best thing to do is ask your doctor or nurse directly: 'Can you explain what you were saying?' You always have the right to know what's going on with your own body, in words that make sense to you. Your parents can help ask too.
I want to go home right now. Can you make them let me go home?

Wanting to go home is one of the most normal feelings in the world when you're in the hospital, and it's okay to really, really want that. The reason you're staying is because your doctors want to make sure you're safe and feeling better before you leave — not to keep you here for no reason. I can't make that decision, but your doctor can explain exactly what needs to happen before you can go home. Sometimes knowing the plan makes the waiting easier. You can ask your nurse: 'What does my body need to do before I can go home?' That way you have something to look forward to.
My tummy hurts from being scared, not from being sick. What do I do?

Your body is really smart — when you're scared or worried, it actually does make your tummy hurt, because your feelings and your body are connected like that. That kind of tummy hurt is real, even if it's not from being sick. There are a few things that might help: taking some slow deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth, asking a nurse for a warm blanket for your belly, or telling your mom or dad how you're feeling so they can sit with you. The Child Life team here at Children's Hospital also helps kids with scary feelings — your nurse can connect you with them.
I don't want to take a bath here. I only like baths at home.

That makes a lot of sense — baths at home feel safe and familiar, and here everything is different. You don't have to have a bath if it doesn't feel right today. You can always do a gentle wash with a warm cloth instead, which lots of kids prefer in the hospital anyway. If there's a specific thing that makes bath time at home feel better — a special soap, a toy you keep in the tub, a certain way things are done — you can tell your nurse and they'll try their best to make it feel more like home. Your comfort matters here.
The other kid in the next room was crying really loud. Will that happen to me too?

It can be hard to hear other kids who are upset — your feelings about that are completely understandable. Every kid at Children's Hospital is here for different reasons, and what's happening for them isn't the same as what's happening for you. Your care team knows your specific situation and they'll always tell you what to expect before anything happens. You'll never be surprised without warning. And if you're ever feeling scared or upset yourself, it's completely okay to show it — crying is one of the ways our bodies let out big feelings, and nobody here will think less of you for it.
I keep having bad dreams since I got here. What do I do?

Bad dreams can happen when our brain is trying to work through something stressful, and being in the hospital is definitely stressful. There are some things that can help: keeping something familiar nearby like a stuffed animal or a blanket from home, having a parent or trusted adult nearby when you fall asleep, and telling your nurse if the bad dreams are really bothering you — they can check if anything, like a medicine or the room lighting, might be making sleep harder. Some kids also find it helps to tell someone about the dream so it feels less powerful. You're safe here, and your team wants you to feel that way even while you sleep.
Why do the doctors talk so quiet when they're outside my door?

You've got sharp ears! Doctors and nurses often talk quietly in the hallway because they're being careful about privacy — there are lots of different patients nearby and they don't want anyone to overhear private things about other people. It's also just a habit they develop to keep the ward calm and peaceful. If they're talking about you and you want to know what they said, you can always ask: 'I heard you talking outside — can you come in and tell me what's going on?' You always have the right to know what's happening with your own care.
Is there wifi here? Can I use it on my tablet?

Yes! Children's Hospital has wifi available for patients and families. Ask your nurse for the network name and password — they'll give it to you. Your tablet should connect just fine. Staying entertained and connected to the things you love is a real part of getting better, so don't feel bad about using it. If you're having trouble connecting, the nurse can help troubleshoot or find someone who can.
What's that big white machine down the hall that goes whooomp?

That sounds like it could be an MRI machine — one of the special machines that takes really detailed pictures of the inside of people's bodies, kind of like a super-powered camera. The whooshing and thumping sounds are made by big magnets spinning around really fast inside it. It looks big and loud but it doesn't hurt. Doctors use the pictures it makes to understand what's going on inside someone's body without having to do anything invasive. Pretty amazing when you think about it!
How come some nurses wear different colours than others?

Great observation! At Children's Hospital, different uniforms can mean different jobs. Nurses, doctors, physiotherapists, and other care team members sometimes wear different colours or badges so you (and everyone else) can tell at a glance who does what. It's a bit like how different sports teams wear different jerseys. If you ever want to know who someone is, you can always look at their badge — it has their name and their role on it. And you can always just ask: 'What do you do here?' Most people are happy to explain.
My bracelet says numbers on it. What do the numbers mean?

Your bracelet is actually really important — it has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. The numbers are a unique code that belongs only to you, kind of like a library card for your hospital stay. Before your nurses give you any medicine, do any tests, or take you anywhere, they scan your bracelet to make absolutely sure everything is meant for you and not for someone else. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps you safe. Don't ever take it off while you're here — and if it gets loose or falls off, tell a nurse right away so they can put a new one on.
Can I keep the stuffed animal the hospital gave me when I leave?

Yes, absolutely — anything given to you during your stay is yours to take home. If a nurse or volunteer gave you a stuffed animal or a toy as comfort, that's a gift and it belongs to you. Some kids like keeping it as a reminder of being brave. You can bring it home, give it a name, put it on a shelf — whatever feels right to you.
Do the doctors go home at night or do they stay here forever?

Doctors do go home — but here's the cool thing: there are always doctors here, day and night, every single day of the year, including holidays. They work in shifts, kind of like how different teams take turns. So the doctor you see in the morning might go home at the end of their shift, but a different doctor takes over and knows all about what's going on with you. Your care team also keeps very careful notes so nothing falls through the cracks when the people change. You are never without a doctor here, even at 3 in the morning.
Why do I have to pee in a cup that's not a toilet?

Peeing in a cup is one of the hospital's ways of looking at what your body is doing on the inside. Pee actually carries a lot of information — it can tell doctors about how your kidneys are working, whether there's an infection, how hydrated you are, and lots of other things. They need to collect it in a clean cup so they can run tests on it in the lab. It feels a bit weird the first time, but the nurses will show you exactly how to do it and give you everything you need. After the test is done, it goes straight to the lab and your results help the doctors take better care of you.
Can other kids come visit me or just my family?

Friends and other kids can visit, but there are some rules about visiting at Children's Hospital to keep everyone safe — including things like how old visitors need to be, whether they've been sick recently, and what time visiting hours are. Your nurse can tell you the current rules for your unit. If you have a specific friend you'd really like to see, ask your parent or nurse to help figure out if and when they can come. Having a friend visit can make a big difference when you're going through something hard.
Is the food here from a real restaurant or does someone cook it in the hospital?

The food at Children's Hospital is cooked right here in the building by a real kitchen team. You'll get to choose from a menu each day, and a tray comes to your room. The kitchen tries to have options for different tastes and needs — if there's something you can't or won't eat, tell your nurse and they can make sure the kitchen knows. It's not quite the same as home cooking, but it's real food made fresh. And your family can bring you snacks from outside too, as long as your care team says it's okay with your current diet.
Can I sleep with the lights on? I don't like the dark in here.

Of course — you can absolutely have a light on. There's usually a small night light in the room that's much softer than the overhead lights, and your nurse can help you find the setting that feels right. Some kids like a little bit of light, some like the overhead off but a lamp on, and some want it fully dark. Your comfort matters and there's no rule that says it has to be dark. Just tell your nurse what you need and they'll set it up for you.
What happens if I accidentally press the button on my bed?

Don't worry — there's no penalty for accidentally pressing a button. If a nurse comes in because you pressed the call button by mistake, just tell them it was an accident and they'll simply check that you're okay and head back. That button is there to help you and nurses would much rather have a false alarm than have you need something and not press it. If you're worried about pressing something you shouldn't, ask your nurse to point out which buttons do what — most of the controls are really simple once someone explains them.
My mom brought my favourite snacks from home. Am I allowed to eat them?

It depends on what your care team has said about your diet. Some kids are on specific diets because of their condition or because they have a test or procedure coming up — in those cases, certain foods need to be approved first. Check with your nurse before eating anything from home, just to be safe. In many cases it's completely fine, and having a taste of something familiar from home can actually really help with how you're feeling. Your nurse just needs to give the go-ahead so it doesn't interfere with your treatment.
Can I wear my own pyjamas instead of the hospital ones?

Yes, in most cases you can wear your own pyjamas or comfortable clothes — most kids actually prefer it. Your care team just needs easy access to wherever an IV or monitor might be attached, so loose-fitting clothes work best. If you're having a procedure that requires a hospital gown, your nurse will let you know ahead of time. Otherwise, bring whatever comfortable clothes from home make you feel most like yourself.
How come they woke me up at night to check on me? I was sleeping.

It's one of the frustrating parts of being in hospital — your nurses need to check on you at regular intervals even during the night because some important things, like your blood pressure or how a medicine is working, need to be monitored on a schedule that doesn't stop for sleep. It's not to bother you — it's because they're taking good care of you. If the overnight checks are making it really hard to sleep, you can talk to your nurse about whether any of them could be adjusted, done more gently, or combined so there are fewer interruptions. Sometimes small changes are possible.
Is my little sister allowed to come visit even though she's only four?

Children can usually visit, but there are specific rules about visitors at Children's Hospital that depend on the unit and the current health situation on the ward. Very young children sometimes have age restrictions on certain floors during things like cold and flu season, to protect patients who might be more vulnerable. Your nurse is the best person to check with — just ask 'My four-year-old sister wants to visit; is that okay on this unit right now?' They'll tell you exactly what the current rules are and what your sister would need to do, like washing her hands and making sure she's not recently been sick.
Do I have to stay in my room the whole time or can I walk around?

Whether you can walk around depends on how you're feeling and what your care team has said. Some kids need to stay in bed or in their room because of their treatment, and some are able to move around the unit. If you're not sure, ask your nurse: 'Am I allowed to walk around?' If you can, there may be a playroom, a common area, or hallways you're welcome to explore. Getting up and moving when it's medically okay is actually a good thing for your body and your mood. Your nurse will let you know what's safe for you specifically.
What time do the lights have to go off at night?

There's no strict 'lights out' rule that applies to every room — it's more about being considerate of others if you're sharing a room. In your own space, you can keep your light on as long as you need to. The hospital does try to keep hallways quieter and dimmer overnight so everyone can rest, but your personal light is your call. If you want to read or use your tablet at night, that's generally fine. Just keep the sound low if you're sharing a room so your neighbour can sleep too.
Can my dad sleep here with me tonight?

Yes — at Children's Hospital, parents and guardians are welcome to stay overnight with their child. There's usually a recliner or pull-out cot in the room for them. If your dad wants to stay, just let your nurse know and they'll make sure he has somewhere comfortable to rest. Having a parent stay the night is really common and the staff are used to it — it can make a big difference in how safe and settled you feel. If there's any reason a specific night might be harder (like a very early procedure), your nurse can help plan around it.
My tablet died and I didn't bring my charger. What do I do?

First, ask your nurse — they often have a collection of common chargers that previous families have left behind, or know where to find one. You can also ask a family member to bring your charger from home. Some units have a charging station or can point you to a nearby one. In the meantime, the hospital has wifi, so if someone can bring a device or charger, you'll be back online quickly. Don't underestimate how much having your own entertainment matters — the staff want you to have it and will usually try to help.
The doctor said I need something called an IV. What even is that and will it hurt?

An IV is a tiny flexible tube that goes into a vein, usually in your arm or hand. Once it's in, it stays there and doesn't move — so medicines or fluids can be given to you without needing a new needle every time. Putting it in does involve one small poke, and your care team will use a special numbing cream first so you feel much less of it. The poke lasts just a second. After that, the IV just sits there and most kids forget it's even there. You're allowed to ask for the numbing cream — it's called EMLA — and it's completely normal to ask for it.
What does it feel like when they put you to sleep for an operation?

When the medicine that makes you sleep goes in — usually through your IV or sometimes as a gas you breathe through a mask — it works really fast, usually in less than a minute. Most kids say it feels a bit like falling asleep on the couch really quickly. You might feel a little floaty or see things get blurry, and then you're asleep. You won't feel any time passing, and when you wake up the operation will already be done. You might feel a bit groggy or confused when you first wake up, and that's completely normal. The anaesthesia team watches over you the whole entire time.
They said I can't eat before the test tomorrow. What if I get really hungry?

Not eating before a test or procedure is called 'fasting,' and there's a real medical reason for it — it keeps you safer while you're having the test or if you need any medicine. It can definitely be uncomfortable if you're used to eating. Tell your nurse what time you stopped eating and when the test is, and they'll make sure you know exactly how long it will be. After the test is done and your care team says you can eat, you'll get to have something right away. If you're feeling really uncomfortable from hunger, let your nurse know — they'll keep track and make sure you're okay.
How come I have to keep wearing this thing on my finger that glows red?

That glowing clip is called a pulse oximeter, and it's completely painless — it just shines a little light through your fingertip to measure two things: how fast your heart is beating and how much oxygen is in your blood. The red glow is just the light doing its job. Doctors use it to check that your body is getting enough oxygen without having to do anything uncomfortable. Some kids think it looks pretty cool, like a tiny red flashlight. You can switch it to a different finger if one feels uncomfortable — just ask your nurse.
My friend had this same test and she said it was really cold and loud. Is that true?

Your friend's experience is real — some tests, especially MRI scans, are cold because the room is kept cool, and loud because the machine makes big thumping sounds when it works. Your care team will tell you specifically what to expect for your test. They can often give you a warm blanket if you're cold, and ear protection or headphones for the noise if the machine is loud. It really helps to know in advance, so you can ask your nurse: 'What will this test feel like and what can I bring or do to make it easier?' They'll give you an honest answer.
Will my parents be in the room when the doctor checks me or do they have to wait outside?

In most cases at Children's Hospital, a parent or guardian can be with you during check-ups and many procedures — especially if you want them there. For some specific tests or parts of examinations, there might be a medical reason a parent needs to step just outside for a moment, but your nurse or doctor will explain why if that happens. If having your parent in the room is really important to you, say so — the team will do their best to make that work. And you're always allowed to have someone with you for support.
After I have the operation, will I feel sick when I wake up?

Some kids do feel a bit nauseous or queasy when they wake up from anaesthesia — it's a known side effect of the sleeping medicine. If it happens to you, it doesn't mean something went wrong; it's just your body adjusting. Your team can give you medicine to help with the sick feeling if it's bothering you, so you don't have to just wait it out. When you wake up you'll be in a special recovery area where nurses watch you closely until you're more alert. They'll ask how you feel and take good care of you right from the moment you open your eyes.
Will I have to stay in my room the whole time or will they take me somewhere?

It depends on what tests or treatments you need. For some things, your care team comes to your room. For others — like X-rays, MRI scans, or surgery — you'll be taken somewhere else in the building on a wheelchair or bed. Before each trip, your nurse will tell you where you're going, how long it takes, and what will happen when you get there. You'll never just disappear to a mystery location without an explanation. And a parent or guardian can often come with you for these trips too, especially for the parts before and after any procedure.
What if I need to go to the bathroom when they're in the middle of doing something to me?

You can always tell the team. Most tests and check-ups can be paused for a bathroom break if needed. Just say 'I need to go to the bathroom' and the team will stop and help you. Before any longer procedure, your nurse will usually ask if you need to go first — but if you forget or it comes up unexpectedly, it's okay to say so. Nobody is going to make you uncomfortable on purpose. And if you have an IV or monitoring equipment, the nurse will help you manage that during the bathroom trip too.
How will I know when it's time to go home? Will someone just come and get me?

Going home is called 'discharge,' and it doesn't happen suddenly without warning. Your doctor will talk to you and your parents before you're discharged and explain what's happening. There are usually some things that need to happen first — like a nurse going through care instructions, and someone making sure your follow-up appointments are set. You'll have time to get your things together. Before you leave you'll get paperwork that explains what to do at home. Nobody will rush you out the door. When the time comes, you'll definitely know.
There's a person who comes in and just writes stuff on a board and leaves. What are they doing?

That's probably someone from your care team updating the whiteboard in your room — those boards usually show things like your nurse's name, important goals for the day, and any scheduled tests or visits. It's a way of keeping everyone who comes into your room informed at a glance, including you and your family. If you want to know who that specific person was, look at their badge the next time they come in. You can also ask your nurse: 'Who's the person who updates the board?' They'll tell you exactly.
Why are there so many different people coming in to see me? How many doctors do I have?

At Children's Hospital you might have more people involved in your care than you'd expect — and it can feel like a lot! Depending on your situation, you might have a main doctor, a specialist or two, a resident who checks on you regularly, nurses for each shift, and other team members like a physiotherapist or dietitian. It's not because something is complicated in a scary way — it's because your hospital has experts for lots of different things. If you want to understand who's who, ask your nurse to introduce the main players: 'Can you tell me the names and jobs of the main people looking after me?'
The person who brought my lunch wasn't wearing the same colour as the nurses. Who are they?

That person is from the food services team — they work in the hospital kitchen and deliver meals to patients. They're an important part of the team even though they're not medical staff. They usually wear a different uniform colour to distinguish their role. If you have a question about your food — like if something doesn't look right or you want something different — you can mention it to them directly or tell your nurse, who can pass along any food preferences or dietary needs to the kitchen team.
There's someone who walked around with a dog today. Is that their pet or a hospital dog?

That's a therapy dog! Children's Hospital has certified therapy dogs who visit patients to provide comfort and a little bit of home. They're brought in by their handlers from programs like St. John Ambulance and go through special training to be calm and gentle around hospital environments. They're not the handler's pet in the regular sense — their job is to visit kids like you. If you'd love a visit from one of the therapy dogs, ask your nurse — they can often arrange for a visit to your room. Lots of kids find it really cheering.
A person asked me how I was feeling but they weren't a nurse. They had a different badge. Who was that?

It might have been a Child Life specialist! They're a special part of the team at Children's Hospital whose job is specifically about how kids are feeling emotionally — not medically. They help kids understand what's happening, deal with scary feelings, and find ways to feel more comfortable and less bored. They're not there to do anything medical at all. If you liked talking to that person and want to see them again, just mention it to your nurse: 'Can the Child Life specialist come back?' They'll arrange it.
Sometimes there's a group of people who all come in together and talk about me. Who are all those people?

That's called a ward round or care round — the group is your medical team checking in together. It usually includes your main doctor, one or more residents or students who are learning, sometimes a pharmacist, and possibly other specialists. They talk through how you're doing and what the plan is for the day. You're allowed to be part of that conversation and ask questions while they're in the room. If it feels confusing to have so many people at once, you can ask your nurse afterward to explain what was discussed in plainer language.
Is there someone I can call if I need something and my nurse is busy?

Yes — the call button next to your bed alerts the nurses' station right away, and even if your specific nurse is occupied with someone else, another member of the nursing team will come to check on you. You're never on your own waiting for just one person. Press the button whenever you need something — it doesn't have to be an emergency. That's what it's there for.
The person who gave me my medicine this morning looks really young. Are they still learning?

They might be a student nurse, a nursing student doing their clinical placement, or a young-looking qualified nurse — it's hard to tell from appearance alone. Nursing students always work under the supervision of a fully qualified nurse, who is responsible for your care. If you're ever unsure who someone is or what their training level is, you're allowed to ask: 'Are you a student or a qualified nurse?' They'll tell you honestly. Your safety is the most important thing, and everything that happens with your care is checked and supervised.
There's a room down the hall with toys and a person who plays games. Can I go there?

That sounds like the playroom or activity room, and the person there is probably a Child Life specialist or recreation therapist — their job is to help kids have fun and feel more normal while they're in hospital. Many kids can visit if their care team says it's okay for them to walk around. Ask your nurse: 'Am I allowed to go to the playroom down the hall?' They'll check what your current plan says and either give you the go-ahead or, if you can't go right now, might be able to arrange for someone from that room to come to you.
What's a physiotherapist? One is coming to see me tomorrow and I don't know what they do.

A physiotherapist — sometimes called a physio or PT — is a specialist who helps people move their bodies well. They're experts in muscles, joints, movement, and recovery. Depending on why you're in hospital, they might help you strengthen muscles, improve balance, learn how to move safely while you're healing, or just get up and walk around when you haven't been moving for a while. Their visits are often one of the more active and hands-on parts of hospital care. They'll explain exactly what they want to do before they do it, and you can always ask questions during the visit.
